SUGGESTED APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER SECURITY MEASURES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion in a case of urgent and pressing necessity. The use of explosives by criminals and mentally unbalanced persons to achieve their perverted ends of political terrorism, private vengeance or other purpose is increasing. In Canada, as elsewhere, the intended victim is often connected with one of the established institutions of society, such as a court of justice, penitentiary, legislature, or other symbol of government. Not only the intended victim is endangered but no one within that particular institution is safe from the indiscriminate blast of the explosive. I need only refer to the recent incident in the courthouse at Winnipeg.
I move the following motion with particular reference to this institution of parliament:
That Mr. Speaker be authorized to meet with the Speaker of the other chamber to select a committee of both Houses to assist them in recommending to both Houses security measures for the protection of the public, the staff, and members in the parliament buildings and surrounding grounds.
And that Mr. Speaker be authorized to communicate this resolution to the Honourable the Speaker of the Senate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege along the lines of the question put by my colleague, the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) and further to the answer given to a question put by him this morning. My question is for the Prime Minister regarding the Law of the Sea Conference. The hon. member for South Shore brought to the attention of the House the fact that a commitment was made and an undertaking given by certain ministers of the Crown having to do with Canada's position at the Law of the Sea Conference. He asked whether or not we would be prepared to take unilateral action to protect our fish resources. The hon. member read from the St. John's Evening Telegram the statement made by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson).
I might draw the attention of the House to the statement made by the previous minister of fisheries who in his official capacity as minister of fisheries issued a statement in Halifax which was later reported in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald issue of June 15 at which time he made the same undertaking. I might add that at the meeting referred to earlier with the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion the Prime Minister was present, so I do not think he can shake it off and say that he was not aware of the promise made.
This is a very important matter which affects the lives, the livelihood and the future prospects of many thousands of Canadians living on the eastern seaboard and on the
October 3, 1974

west coast of Canada. I take strong exception to these people being misled, and I might add maybe deliberately misled, by ministers of the Crown who for political purposes or political expediency promised tbe people of Canada, the people of Newfoundland and people in other parts of Canada that this action would be taken, in the full knowledge that this government would not support the action if Canada's position was not improved at the Law of the Sea Conference.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, transportation problems in Canada remain a present-day issue. There was talk about it during the last election. The Speech from the Throne reflected a large part of the public discussions which took place during the election campaign, and we intend to continue the discussions and implement the proposed measures.

October 3, 1974
The Address-Hon. J. Marchand
During the summer, Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity to read perhaps with closer attention the history of Canada as related to the development of railways, and I had the pleasure to read among other things that great book by Pierre Berton the National Dream, and The Last Spike. And I had never realized, Mr. Speaker, how closely the history of the development of Canada was related to the development of the railways. The whole development of western Canada is interrelated with the development of the railways. Furthermore, if one reads the first debates that followed the creation of this beautiful country that is ours, one realizes that railways were a focal concern of politicians of that time.
Sir John A. Macdonald spent a great deal of his political life trying to solve the railway problem in Canada, or rather build a railway that would link eastern and western Canada. So the problem of transportation is undoubtedly vital to any country but particularly for Canada. Because of the vastness of the Canadian territory, differing areas which are so far apart, it is essential that this country be linked by the best means of transportation known.
So it is not surprising that even in 1974 there is still talk about the transportation policy, new means to link Canadians, setting up faster and easier communications so that our country will be more united.
There is no doubt that the unity of this country is impossible without an excellent transportation system, not only for passengers, but also for goods. Transportation in Canada includes not only railways, but also transportation by bus, by car, by boat, by airplane. This includes airports and seaports, which means that the greater part of Canadian activity is related to the development of our transportation policy.
I am therefore happy, Mr. Speaker, that the government has decided to make a special effort to make the required improvements, and there are many of them. Regardless of any statement that can be made, I am convinced that many things should be changed. I just read the speech that I made last March, Mr. Speaker, and there is not a single sentence in it that needs to be changed, despite any direct or indirect accusation that may have been made. I am not speaking of my friends opposite, but of other people more directly involved in transportation. Transportation is directly related to the public interest. This is why, Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, no individual, no private company should have an advantage over the government in the development of transportation.
I would not want it to be said, Mr. Speaker, that I suggest that the government should acquire all transportation means in Canada; this is not at all what I want. I believe this would be the greatest mistake we could make. There are several other areas where we can invest our money, but I believe that the general transportation policy must be developed by the government and followed by all those who work in the transportation field and who have a right to make a profit in this field as long as their search for profit is in the interest of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we have already started to make some changes. We have already developed some plans.


We signed a bilateral air agreement with the United States. We allocated routes to the carriers.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not very well.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If ever you want to discuss them I am ready any time. There is an airline in this country which belongs to the citizens of Canada, so if some people on the other side of the House do not like that they should say so publicly. I am sure they are never going to be elected on such a platform.
We have signed this agreement. We have adopted the Darling rates on coastal trade. We have met again and again with the Atlantic provinces on freight rates so that we can develop that part of the country more than it has been in the past. The committee of western ministers on transportation has worked well.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Who told you that?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I think some members on the other side of the House have met those ministers and have seen how seriously they do their work. They are interested in transportation, in the problems of Canada, and not in politicking, as some are.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Of course, you never indulge in that, do you?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I don't know why some members are not happy when something good happens to Canadians. The ministers are satisfied. We are working together and solving problems. We meet in a cheerful and non-partisan atmosphere.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, boy!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why is the hon. member so sad about that?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You will strain your wrist patting yourself on the back.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
You are quite an adviser, George.
We are experimenting in Ontario with the Richmond Hill to Toronto commuter train, which is important but only a start. The STOL program, which is being developed rapidly, has become a real success.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are seeing a repetition of what happened a few minutes ago. When something works well, members opposite are unhappy. I don't understand.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Who's unhappy? We are surprised.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

No, that it works at all.
October 3, 1974

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: This is a very important program.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I sincerely regret interrupting the minister who is making an excellent speech. Will he permit a question now or at the end of his speech about the STOL program?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will answer the question before the hon. member puts it. I think the hon. member wants to know if Mr. Sinclair was right in saying that the STOL program cost $135 million. Mr. Sinclair is wrong. Is the hon. member satisfied? As I said previously, the program cost $25 million. That is the correct figure, and not the one suggested by Mr. Sinclair. I don't know why he said that. Of course, that $25 million figure does not cover everything carried in the budgets of all the different departments concerned.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What is the total?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We are talking about STOL.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You are stalling.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You don't know.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do know, but I am not going to mention it, for obvious reasons. I am being perfectly honest. I am telling members the plain truth, but I am not going to reveal all the details. I repeat, the figure of $25 million which I mentioned previously is the right one. If Mr. Sinclair contends the STOL program has cost $135 million, let him prove what he says. I think he is wrong. He should not consider himself as speaking for the government of Canada. He is speaking as a citizen, and that is all. My interest in this is no smaller than his.
We are already on the way to transforming and improving transportation throughout Canada. Here I shall mention the CNR Turbo train which runs between Ottawa and Montreal and Montreal and Toronto. The Canadian Pacific Railway is about to enter into service a train which will be a bit faster. We hope that company will change its policy. Why do I say that? A few years ago everybody in Canada, including the railways, thought we should eliminate passenger trains.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not everybody.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Everybody thought we should use cars.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I didn't.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
People thought that motor cars and airplanes were the vehicles of the future. Now, people notice that this is not so. I do not say cars will disappear from our highways or that aircraft will not fly. I do say that there are plans for improved passenger train service. We want people to be happy to travel by train instead of by car. It should not take two or three hours, as happens now, to go from St. Hyacinthe to Montreal if you leave at nine o'clock in the morning. That is awful! We can do better than that.
The railways have given a commitment to improve services. In the election campaign and in the Speech from the
The Address-Hon. J. Marchand
Throne we said that the government intends to create a corporation for operating passenger trains. We still support the idea, as announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the west. We are not anxious to do this. It is not our first priority. We will say this to the railways: "You contend you know the business better than we do. Show us how good you are. Demonstrate to us that you can improve the service to a greater extent than we could if we were to create a corporation." We have not abandoned the idea but want to give the railways a chance to show they can do better than we can, as a government. There is no rush to create a corporation, but there is a rush to improve passenger train service.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when you deal with transportation, it is like being in a restaurant. Some are interested in the food, some in reading the menu and some in changing the cook. I am interested in having good food on the table, that is, in good train service for transporting people and enough cars to carry our goods, so that we can export manufactured products and create good service to our ports. This holds true particularly for Vancouver and some parts of eastern Canada. This is what I am interested in and the government is ready to take all legal and moral measures to achieve this result. We do not want to be unnecessarily doctrinaire. We do not intend to do things just one way and say there is only one way of doing them. There are several ways of doing things. We know that. We are ready to be flexible but we will not be flexible in reaching the objectives defined during the election campaign and the Speech from the Throne. [Translation]
Now, Mr. Speaker, we have a vast country-as is well known and, evidently, I have not discovered it-and some of its regions are isolated. We must therefore find a way to bring these regions closer so as to provide them with communication and transportation facilities in order to allow Canadians to live everywhere on the Canadian territory and not only in Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver or Calgary. Some people are living in the far north, others in remote communities. Ways must be found to enable them to travel fast and in comfort, so that they may thus contemplate living either at the place where they were born or where they have elected to settle down.
But how should it be done? The plane seems to be most appropriate to that end. This means that we will have to launch a program for the development of small airports from which we could reach by air nearly any place in Canada, especially where there is no other available means.
This is another area where improvements are to be introduced, clearly within eventual budget restrictions, because such a program may cost billions. Everything then will depend on the government's general economic policy, the fight against inflation and so on. We will however proceed with all due speed, in order that Canada may have the best transportation system.
We propose to develop navigation in the north because we know natural resources are there and the world will need them. This is common knowledge, after such painful experiences. Why not then give Canada better specializa-
70

October 3, 1974
The Address-Hon. J. Marchand tion in far north shipping? Why not have better ice-breakers, better ice-going ships. All this belongs to us, here in Canada, and we will have to specialize in that field.
We have a program for developing navigation in the north. Speaking of navigation in the north and coastal shipping-that is water transport from one point to another in Canada-it will be done in the future by Canadian ships with Canadian crews. And with our existing lake-going fleet, we already have the elements of a merchant navy large enough for Canada. We will then have to look.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is the merchant marine.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is part of the merchant marine. It is not complete because we still do not have ocean going ships. This is something I hope we will have in the future.
There is not only the problem of inter-city communication, but urban transportation. This is in the provincial and municipal field, not the federal field. However, we are ready to co-operate as we are doing with the provinces and municipalities in order to solve this very serious problem of urban transportation. This can only be done through co-operation because we do not have any specific jurisdiction in that field. This is a problem that must be solved because it is becoming more and more impossible to live in certain large cities because of the poor transportation system. We are offering our co-operation to the provinces and the municipalities in order to improve this situation.
We want more information about transportation. We do not have all the information. As hon. members know, private enterprise is involved. There are bus companies, private railways and provincially-owned railways. We will be asking the House to adopt an information act of some kind in order that we may get all the information.
We now have a commitment from the railways that they will supply, at the request of the Canadian Transport Commission, all information that is asked for by the provinces. We were asked for this by the provinces previously, but unfortunately the election prevented us from doing anything about it. The provinces have asked us to amend the Railway Act so that we not only have a promise from one man or one board of directors. The provinces want to have a definite right. If the opposition parties are interested, I think an amendment to the Railway Act can be passed compelling the railways to supply information at the request of the Canadian Transport Commission or the Department of Transport.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There is also the problem of freight rates. We are still discussing with the western provinces what criteria should be established for freight rates in Canada. Are we going to use the railways as an instrument for regional development? This will have to be defined so we know exactly what we want to do. The railways are costing the Canadian people a lot of money. In the passenger field alone, the cost is $100 million a year.

That is a lot of money and I think the government and this House should have some say in this.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I read this morning that some people contend we do not have to change anything, that everything is O.K. in the transportation act of 1967. However, that is not the way we feel. I regret to say we think it is far from being perfect. Even though it costs a lot of money to maintain our railways, the general public profits by it. For example, I am sure the Richmond Hill-Toronto commuter train will not make a profit, but the whole community will profit. If two or three thousand people save two or three hours a day, that is worth a lot of money and must be taken into account.
Even though what we propose will involve a lot of money, if that is transposed at the national accounts level, it will be seen that it is probably the best way to save money. I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) agrees. I see he is leaving.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I wish to make one more point. I've really just begun my speech.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Carry on.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I want to underline one point, the problem of consultation.

Consultation is very important in this field. If there is a field where things are cut up, it is that of transport. You have provinces which make the roads. Private companies like the bus companies. There are national companies, like the Canadian National, not to mention the Canadian Pacific and the airlines. There are municipal jurisdictions, provincial jurisdictions, private interests and Crown corporations. As we look at the whole, we come to the conclusion that it cannot work unless there is a state of permanent coordination and consultation between all the agencies concerned.
There are towns where you might have an excellent air service, perfect roads and train and bus systems that are quite up-to-date. There are other places, however, where there is nothing of all that; so there is going to have to be coordination so that everything is not concentrated in the same place. And, if our means are limited, well then, let us try to spend and invest our money so that the greatest possible number of Canadians can benefit by all known modern transportation means.
I do not want to start a discussion in the House, Mr. Speaker, but I remember very well that there once was an air company that abandoned a small line in the west. Today, they have a bus to replace this and they would not want to go back to the old system because they found that they saved much more time this way. As far as we are concerned, we find that with the small STOL aircraft between Montreal and Ottawa a lot of time is saved even if the aircraft flies a bit slower.
We need some sort of total planning which cannot be exclusively brought about by the federal government but

by all the provincial governments as well as the municipal governments when it comes to urban transport.
So we will have to discuss these problems. It will not be easy because I know this will be extremely expensive. Recently I spent a few days in England and France. I remember that after the war when I went to France for the first time, I was shocked by the bad rail service. Of course, the war was somehow responsible for that situation, but today their trains are more comfortable than ours, and it is the same thing in England. Why do people use trains? Because those trains are comfortable and fast.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Whose fault is it?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Whose fault is it? Anyone who wants to make a trial can do so. But I am here to build trains, so I will try to do just that. Everybody will be working. I will be busy with the railroads while others make trials.
Anyway, Mr. Speaker, I simply wanted to point to the House that the good feelings we had expressed concerning transport, passenger services, freight transport, freight rates, lack of discrimination-
We still believe in all this. Even though the election is over and we have a majority here, we believe in it-even more so, if possible. We are in a good position, now, even if hon. gentlemen opposite are not happy, to do all the good things Canadians are waiting for us to do.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the minister if he will agree to answer. It is stated in the Speech from the Throne that the government intends to establish machinery to ensure the effective management of all ground transportation. Would the minister elaborate on this proposal and tell us what is meant by the statement to which I have just referred?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order. The minister's time has expired and I would not wish him to embark on any lengthy explanation, though he may wish to reply briefly.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be brief. I think we will develop our transport policy as we go along. The Speech from the Throne mentions a corporation for passenger cars and a corporation for rail cars to assure an adequate supply of those. More problems will arise as we go along, but we are determined to take all the means necessary to realize the goals we have set, and we do not have to bother with a full list of those means.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure for me to hear the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) even though, in matters affecting transport, he sometimes allows his imagination to take the place of facts. He is a remarkable orator, one
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
who enlivens the House, and I have always tried to be present whenever he speaks. Whether I agree with him or not, he has developed that undefinable parliamentary quality to such an extent over the years that I always enjoy hearing him speak even though, when he has finished, we have little or no idea of what he was actually endeavouring to prove.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
However, I say in all sincerity that I have great admiration for him as I have for all hon. members who endeavour to express themselves clearly and with honesty of purpose. I cannot say more of anyone than that. I did notice, though, that in his praise for himself and his department in connection with the allotment of air routes from the United States he forgot the province of Saskatchewan. This is not the first time Saskatchewan has been forgotten, particularly since it turned to the former allies and bedfellows of the Liberal government during the last parliament. When they ceased to support the government, Saskatchewan was forgotten.
Furthermore, I should like to have heard the minister say something more about the transportation of oil and gas by railroad from the north. This matter has been thoroughly looked into by the Queen's University Committee which came to the conclusion that such a railroad would cost no more than a pipeline and that the environmental difficulties inherent in a pipeline would be completely eliminated. What has been done in that connection?
I should also have liked to have heard the minister say something about the Canadian Transport Commission. This Commission, during the last several years, has brought in recommendations and decisions which, in several cases, have been entirely unmindful of the average Canadian. I think of the recent acceptance by the Commission of the application on the part of Bell Telephone which in my opinion was unjustified and could not be justified. It can only have the effect of stoking still further the inflationary fires in this country.
Now, I wish to deal with one or two matters of particular interest to me arising out of the Speech from the Throne. It was a speech grandiloquent in words, outstanding the sentiment and completely devoid of any serious effort to meet the problems facing Canada today. It was designed to delude the people of Canada into believing that a government which has been sound asleep since the election has suddenly ended its hibernation and that things are being done. Where, in that Speech, is there anything which will help Canadians today? It is beyond me why in all the circumlocution of that Speech there is nothing which meets the major problem facing this country, that is to say, inflation. When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) dealt with inflation throughout the campaign, calling it the number one danger facing our country, he was ridiculed. Now there is suddenly a recognition that such a thing as inflation does exist. It is still apparent that the sloth and inaction of the past weeks, months and, indeed, the last year and a half is what will continue to guide this government.
28305-6V2

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
Government expenditures are on the increase and there is no attempt at control. Budgetary expenditures on September 26 totalled $9.2 billion, some $1,800 million more than the same period in the previous year. Where is this nation going? I am not going to get into a discussion of inflation as it no doubt will be dealt with at length during this debate, but I do suggest that this government could have acted.
What is the government's excuse now? It says it is waiting for the budget. We have had budgets and budgets over and over again during the last three or four years with nothing to meet the serious situation of inflation. As I listened to the unveiling of the Speech from the Throne I could only come to the conclusion that its purpose was simply to becloud the fact that our financial situation in Canada is very serious and to put the blame on international causes when at least 55 per cent of inflation here in Canada is the result of inaction on the part of this government.
Why has there not been some action taken? There is nothing to prevent the government of Canada, even without a budget, from doing something about the awful interest rates which today make it virtually impossible for people in all walks of life to continue. The government has the power to do something and does not have to wait for a budget. Why does it not act now?
I remember very well that when I was Prime Minister the great banking institutions of Canada came to me seeking my agreement to legislation removing the 6 per cent ceiling on interest. I asked them what their purpose was, and they said it was to make the financial situation more flexible. I asked them whether they intended to use such legislation and they said no, at which time I said that under the circumstances my answer was no.
People in Canada today are aroused as never before. The government won an election and boasts of it. I do not object to that feeling of exhilaration that comes from victory, but where is Canada going? If it is going to follow what is set out in the throne speech I wonder what the consequences will be?
This brings me to something that happened on Monday on Parliament Hill. I stood against violence weeks ago when the situation at Kenora showed a degree of dangerous chaos. I said that those who were raising the trouble among the Indians were not the responsible ones but were troublemakers obtaining their inspiration from the United States. What happened here on Parliament Hill will be known throughout the world as an indication that we in this nation are in no different position than other nations, many without the same background and tradition of respect for law.
However, I must add that the government of Canada must bear a large share of the responsibility for what happened as a result of its inaction and the official decision that the minister would not meet with the Indians without the meetings being subject to certain qualifications he wished to impose. That is not the way to deal with difficulties and problems, and certainly not the way to deal with the first race of our country.

I have no sympathy for what these people did, but when I heard that the government refused to meet with them, as it was reported, I feared for the consequences. As an indication of how serious this matter is let me point out that yesterday the Lieutenant Governor of Alberta, himself a full-blooded Cree, speaking with the magnificent record he has had during the years, to the benefit of his people, spoke out strongly and definitively. That is an unusual thing for a representative of Her Majesty, provincially or otherwise.
I say to the government through you, Sir, that I have no consideration for the irresponsible individuals involved, but the vast majority of the Indian race whose contributions to this country have been tremendous and law abiding deserve more than the consideration they have been given to date. I would go further by asking whether the use of the RCMP on Parliament Hill on Monday was a course in keeping with the traditions of the force and the excellent relationship that has prevailed between that force and the Indian peoples?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext: The House has heard the order proposed moved, I take it, by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) and seconded by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang). Shall it be so ordered?

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say very briefly that there have been the usual interesting exchanges among the House leaders. Because the government got itself into an unfortunate predicament and had to be defeated last May 8, it is now in the position where procedures have to be adopted to deal with the 1974-75 main estimates which, together with Governor General's warrants-which I see the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) has before him in large quantities- have almost been expended. So we are prepared to accommodate the government. I want to say, in light of the rather extraordinary claim the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made yesterday for further streamlining and thereby loss of opposition privileges, that when the government is in a position where it needs assistance, there is always on an individual basis a willingness to co-operate. This is what is being done now. As time goes on, I am sure the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) will see how much more co-operation he receives from government House leaders than he did when he was in his other occupation dealing with people at the United Nations.
There is another matter which I think I should mention. The three days which will be devoted to discussion of the estimates in the House will be without interruption either by the opposition attempting to make use of Standing Order 26 or by the government bringing in large clutches of government statements to be made on motions by ministers. This will give the House, and particularly members who have come here since 1968, an opportunity to see how
Estimates
this House can operate in what will be an atmosphere and climate resembling the old committee of supply. We hope ministers will bring forward the details of their estimates without any sins of omission or commission, and that we will have an interesting debate. I say this because it may well be that in the discussion of our rules this procedure will serve as a pilot plan for the proposition this party will make so that we can work out a system of reverting, at least in part, to the old committee of supply rules.

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker I wish to confirm the fact that the motion presented by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) does represent an agreement arrived at among the four House leaders. If some members think that not sufficient time is allowed for debate of these estimates, and others think there is too much time, I can tell them that the amount of time in the motion represents a compromise.
I believe the point made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) should be emphasized, namely, that what we are dealing with here is not a brand new set of estimates but, rather, estimates for the current fiscal year, seven months of which have already been voted or approved in one way or another, most of which has already been spent. It seems, therefore, that we should handle the discussion of these estimates with as much expedition as possible. I feel the arrangement worked out by the House leaders in bringing in this motion takes into account all the important factors.
Perhaps there is one other element in the so-called agreement, among others, which should be mentioned. It should be understood that during the three days October 23, 24 and 25 when we are debating the estimates on the floor of the House, most, if not all, of that time will be spent, in committee of the whole so that there can be an honest back and forth discussion of these estimates.
On behalf of my party, I wish to support this motion. [Translation]

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to confirm what the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) has said, that there was unanimous agreement between the House leaders of the four parties. We took part in the discussions and we endorse it completely for it meets a need we have often stated in this House that the spending of the taxpayer's money was not discussed sufficiently in the House. This agreement provides for three days' discussions in Committee of the Whole, with addi-tionnal sittings, which constitutes some kind of compromise as was said previously. Some would say it is not enough, others that it is too much. To my mind, it is one step towards more effective and better planned procedures in the short and the long term.
I sincerely hope. Mr. Speaker, that there will be more agreements of this type to make House business more effective and better adapted to current needs. These would give each member the opportunity of putting forward his ideas and of checking on the present administration.

subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES AND SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A) FOR YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1975
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the main estimates that I table today are identical to those which were introduced in the last session of the previous Parliament. Hon. members will recall undoubtedly that the examination of that budget was nearly completed by most standing committees at the time Parliament was dissolved.
In March last, the Commons voted interim supplies for the period from April to June inclusive. For the four following months, from July to October, the government obtained its operating funds through special warrants as authorized under the Financial Administration Act. The funds provided in those warrants should meet government needs only until the end of October. I trust that by that time Parliament will have voted all the necessary votes for the current fiscal year. For that matter, Mr. Speaker, agreement was reached on that a moment ago.
Nearly all budget items for which special warrants were issued were already included in the estimates under study when Parliament was dissolved.
The supplementary estimates that I also table today provide for the issuance of special warrants for any budget items not provided for in the main estimates. They also cover expenditures to be incurred in weeks to come to subsidize consumer oil product prices as well as the price of wheat for Canadian consumption. The amounts required to subsidize consumer oil product prices represent 90 per cent of the supplementary estimates.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES AND SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES (A) FOR YEAR ENDING MARCH 31, 1975

I understand the gratitude which the minister feels at being in his present position and not in the one he held previously. As a result, he has probably forgotten to let us have copies of the supplementary estimates which usually come to us, or copies of the statement. I let it pass for that reason, although I think I should file a caveat at this time, on behalf of our party, that if on examination of those supplementary estimates we discover in them any dollar items or votes of expenditure covering some of the lavish promises in money which

the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his friends were flinging around during the course of the election campaign-such as the Toronto park, of which the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) is aware-we will reserve the right to deal with them. speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time of the adjournment, which now seems like a millennium ago, I was dealing with the situation on Parliament Hill. I had mentioned that I felt, disagreeing to the utmost with resorting to violence, that the government must assume considerable responsibility for the manner in which, from the time this group left Vancouver, the government continued to vacillate and did not take action. I

mentioned the RCMP and rather questioned the use of that body for the kind of action it was engaged in here on Parliament Hill. Indeed, when I was prime minister I refused to permit the RCMP to be used for strike breaking in Newfoundland because I felt that that body should not be used in any way, directly or indirectly, which was inconsistent with its tradition.
Now, sir, I intend to say a word or two regarding parliament, and in particular some of the changes that have taken place in the last few months. I mentioned that there had been changes. As one looks at the government front bench, one cannot but be impressed by the fact that today you are a minister and, with your government still in office, tomorrow you are not. It is a case of in again and out again. The only one who ever found a way to get back again was the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey).
I think of the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) who brought many votes to the Liberal Party in the election. I remember him being spoken of by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in words of adulation and eulogy which could only lead one to believe that he was a minister who was certainly in the best graces of the Prime Minister. But out he went. Then there is the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury). He, too, was in that delightful position. He was a minister of national revenue who had performed in a way that met the praise of the Prime Minister and other ministers. He is gone.
Then you think of one or two others who disappeared, and one can only think of the Biblical words, "greater love hath no man than this"-that he lay down the portfolios of his friends for his own survival.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is the strangest thing I have ever known. If I were to use the language that might be used by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in reference to the chickens of two years ago, I would say "the slaughter of the innocents". It is all because for some reason the Prime Minister decided they must go. However, there is another minister who apparently saved himself by his tears, and I know he will identify himself immediately.
I congratulate the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) on his victory in his constituency. I will always defend my brother members in my own province, so I was deeply concerned by the reply given to Douglas Fisher by the Minister of Agriculture when asked how things were going. Mr. Fisher said that when he asked the minister about his party's prospects, he was his usual candid self and said, "If the Prime Minister would send Otto Lang off to China on a mission, things would be better". The interesting thing is that he did not go, Mr. Speaker, and I saw the two of them sitting together, placed there no doubt by the Prime Minister because of this little interlude. I can only conclude that great are the uses of victory because there they sit, cheek by jowl.
I am concerned about the way in which the Minister of Justice, in giving some legal opinions on what should be done, is not only being overawed but overruled by the Prime Minister. He will recall various incidents, but I remember the one on June 24 when the FLQ kidnappers of Mr. Cross were found in Paris. The Minister of Justice said that he did not see any difficulty in extraditing them.
October 3, 1974

He said the prisoners were originally sent to Cuba in exchange for Mr. Cross, but that did not protect them in other countries. An hour or two later, the Prime Minister said it would not be this government's plan to take steps for extradition. That must have been an awful setback for the Minister of Justice.
Parliament is a great place, Mr. Speaker. I never get over my admiration for the place or my interest in it because of incongruities such as I have mentioned that happen with great regularity on that side of the House.

speechtext: Remember 1962.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Otto, you just sit quiet.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Oh, I am glad to have Otto's participation. I have two or three more here, but I did not want to use them because he was so jovial with me today. As I have said on other occasions, when you come to parliament on your first day, or indeed during your first six months, you wonder how you ever got here. After that you wonder how the other 263 members were elected. In this place there is strong argument, but nonetheless there is respect and regard for the integrity of those who sit opposite. Above all, I am interested in seeing the quality of the members who come to this House after every election.
I am not being perfunctory when I say that the mover and seconder of the address in reply performed their duty admirably, difficult as it must have been, when measured by reason, to say the things that they said. I admire those who can speak in both languages with the facility displayed by so many. I recall that the former member for Prince Albert, also the then prime minister of Canada, had a wonderful hold in the province of Quebec. He made only two speeches in French in his years in office. Once he said "oui" and the second time "oui, oui". That had a tremendous effect. When I listen to those who are able to speak in both languages, I have a deep sense of regret for never having been able to do it. I understand what is said. When I try to reply, the quality of my French is such that nobody, from Vancouver Island to Newfoundland, who does not speak French understands. That is trilingualism, as practised in Prince Albert.
Speaking seriously about the Prime Minister's speech-I wish he were here; I know how busy he always is when I speak-he said parliament must be the heart of the nation. I did not read Hansard this morning, so I must depend on memory. Mr. Speaker, who was it who drove a dagger into the heart of parliament when the rule changes were forced through by closure two or three years ago in this House? Those rule changes turned this House into a puppet, to be pushed around by the Prime Minister and those associated with him.
When the so-called reform of the rules of parliament began under Mr. Pearson and was continued under the present Prime Minister, I stood against most of the changes and was virtually alone. Many of my colleagues fell for the argument that parliament must be made more efficient. That is always the Machiavellian argument used when parliament is about to be emasculated. I can tell the House this about the proposed rule changes: as far as I am
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker concerned they will not pass unless they are based upon the principle that we in the opposition have rights, as well as the government.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am glad to see the Minister of Justice applauding.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is what the Prime Minister said.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I think we all know how the minister voted last time. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand) always approves of strengthening parliament.
When the Prime Minister spoke, he did so in solemn tones saturated with sacrament. He spoke feelingly of his high regard for members of parliament. But, Mr. Speaker, I have a good memory. What manner of changed thinking has come over the Prime Minister who on July 26, 1969, said that members were nobodies! Well, the nobodies of 1969 became the subject of his appreciation in 1974. Then he spoke of some of his fellow members in the Liberal Party. Once he said, "I think we will get rid of some of them; they are bums." Some of them who were here in those days are still here.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Some of them just came back.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
One hon. member said that they have just returned. They have returned while yet the light holds forth and burns. It is interesting to note the attitude taken in the last few weeks by some great American papers toward the parliamentary system. They pay the system great tribute. I will not quote because my time is limited. They said, in so many words, that so long as the representatives of the Crown live true to their oaths of office, there cannot be a Watergate in Canada. That was a tremendous tribute to our parliamentary system. The Americans, in attempting to get away from the British parliamentary system, made the president an all powerful king who might believe, as some of his predecessors did, that he is above the law.
In successive amendments to the rules of this House we have lost control of a basic right which is fundamental to parliament-the right to the fullest examination of expenditures. Today there is no such right. Despite all the gyrationS'-we witnessed this afternoon, one cannot get around the situation that there are estimates unpassed from the previous parliament. The first thing we must do is this: we must return to this House, as a committee of the whole, the right to examine ministers on their shortcomings and on their achievements.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I know the attitude of ministers. I have seen it from both sides. When ministers came to me and said, "My estimates are coming up before the House," I said, "You had better be right." There is none of that today. There is virtually no control over the profligate wastefulness in the spending of money. That wastefulness has characterized, in the last six or seven years, the government of this country. Expenditures of ministers, wasteful beyond words, have been unchallengeable in the House. You cannot move a motion against an individual

October 3, 1974
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
item of expenditure except in those few last hours when the matter comes before the House, as happened three years ago when the House voted expenditures of $18 billion between 8.30 at night and 1.30 in the morning.
The first thing that must be restored to parliament is this right: that ministers shall stand in their places and shall be questioned individually in this chamber, sitting in committee, on their expenditures.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If that right were in existence, do you think that the Prime Minister would have spent $95,000 refurbishing his summer residence; that there would have been an expenditure on the official residence, 24 Sussex Drive, of a quarter of a million dollars; that the centre block office would have been refurbished at a cost of $61,000? That would not have taken place if in this chamber we had the right to vote against such expenditures. And so on I could go on the subject of waste and extravagance.
Under my government, the total expenditure was around $6 billion. It is now four times that amount. There is no control whatsoever. When the Prime Minister is soliloquizing about parliament, let him make that change in our rules. I do not care about limitation of time in which to discuss, but I think it is necessary to make changes. However, if the Prime Minister seriously wants to restore parliament, the acceptance of that suggestion which is traditional in our country would do more than all the verbal promises and exhortations in which any of us may indulge.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to advise the right hon. member that his time has expired.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Continue.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I had no idea of the time I had left; because I have been interrupted. I express to the House my deep appreciation.
The Prime Minister says the question period should be improved. I am not at all convinced that oral questions have not arrived at the point where they bear no relationship to the necessity of being answered immediately. We have spread this period out and out. When I first came here, if there were two or three questions before orders of the day, that would be it. One of the reasons for the lengthy question period today is that this government will not answer questions that are put on the order paper.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
They simply leave them there. Time goes on. From session to session and parliament to parliament, they remain unanswered. What should be done is this. Starred questions should be answered in three days, at the outside. Other questions should be answered within four or five days. If that were done, it would save a great deal of time for the House in the three-quarters of an hour

or hour before orders of the day. Will it be done? Will we be able to get answers to questions?
I wish to refer to one example of how the government answers the opposition. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) is not a provocative person. Some others around me are. I have been in his position. He asked an ordinary question today. Did he get an answer from the Prime Minister? He was simply playing around. Absolute power is a wonderful thing, as long as it is not used absolutely. That is what was shown here today. I want to give a prize example, for the benefit of those members who just came into the chamber. On February 28, 1972, the Leader of the Opposition asked a question of the Prime Minister. It was not of a nature that should arouse one at all. After he decided he would listen to what was being asked, the Prime Minister said:
That was your God-damned question.
That is in Hansard. That is not parliamentary language. If it is, this institution will certainly not live. When you think of all that could be done by parliament, with all the ability that is here, when you finally come down to it it is the government that decides whether or not it is going to live up to parliament. Your Honour has been in the chair for three days. It is not for me to say anything of a flattering nature. All I say to you is this: the manner in which you have discharged your responsibilities assures that you will indeed be a spokesman for all members of this House.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Let us together restore parliament.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The government House leader
applauded. If he, in his august and high position as leader in the House, will translate that applause into actuality in the rules, his arrival at that position will be marked as a forward day in the history of parliament.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do not expect answers to be so full as to cover everything under the sun, but I do expect them to be handed down and, above all, to be true. If we together bring about reform of the House and its rules, no one will be a more enthusiastic supporter than me. However, if the House leader brings in any substitute, caricature change in order to gain for the government more and more power, to the absolute exclusion of the opposition, parliament will in fact cease effectively to exist.
The Prime Minister said he was going to reform the Senate. Whenever he is in difficulty, he thinks of things to be done to take the eyes of the people off the problems that face the country. I remember very well when Mr. King defeated me in Prince Albert in the election of 1926. The major part of his policy was that he was going to reform the Senate. In sepulchral tones he spoke of that body. He said, "We are going to put an end to it." He secured the consent of everyone he appointed to the Senate that they would agree to their own dissolution. When in 1940 we asked to see those consents, he said they
October 3, 1974

were personal. The only change was that he substituted live Grits for dead Tories: that was the total reform.
I can see the Minister of Justice avidly thinking of the Senate. I cannot hear his judicial words. We now have a new promise. The Prime Minister is giving a sop to the opposition. If any old Tories in the other place die, he will appoint Tories in their place. That is reform. With support amounting to 85 per cent in the Senate, that statement on his part is indicative of the degree of his desire to bring about the change of which he speaks.
Then there is the question of constitutional reform. During the election campaign the Prime Minister spoke critically of the government of Quebec for having brought in Bill 22. I was able to quote him. In my opinion, it was the worst action which could have been taken in relation to national unity. All over Canada the doctrine of bilingualism was accepted. Now, the province of Quebec turns its back on that doctrine and says: It can apply elsewhere but it is not going to apply here.
What should be done? I would have thought a government with courage would have disallowed that legislation as being unconstitutional. Let the Minister of Justice not tell me it is constitutional, because the godfather of constitutionalism in the Senate, Senator Forsey, says it is entirely unconstitutional. So does Frank Scott. Well, the excuse now being given for not disallowing the bill is that the disallowing process is dead.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am glad the Minister of Justice indicates that he does not hold the view to which I have referred, because the statement he made recently was this: as far as the legislation passed respecting oil in Alberta and Saskatchewan is concerned, if necessary it will be disallowed. So disallowance is still a constitutional possibility, or was only a matter of six months ago. Now the Prime Minister tells us he intends to ride the horse of constitutional reform, that he intends to patriate the constitution and make it truly Canadian. Mr. Speaker, every word and line in the British North America Act of 1867 was prepared in Canada by Canadians before it was ever sent to the British parliament for ratification.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Then he says that if he cannot do it by agreement, he will resurrect-he did not use the word "resurrect" because he does not use Biblical expressions- if he could not do it by agreement, he would resurrect the Victoria charter. Sir, the premier of Quebec was wiser than all the other premiers when he refused to accept the Victoria charter while it was up for ratification and acceptance. What would have happened to us in western Canada if it had gone through? I am surprised the premier of Saskatchewan and the premier of Manitoba accepted it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not the present premier.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: Thatcher?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

I was just about to pay a tribute to the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) on
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker becoming acting leader, but because of this interruption I shall have to omit doing so.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

There is a section in there which emasculates the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba by providing for a certain population basis affecting the four western provinces. In Manitoba and Saskatchewan our populations are declining. We would be the only two provinces under the Victoria charter to be placed in a secondary position had that proposal gone through. I hope the Prime Minister will not try to bring back that charter.
Something else is to be brought about. Apparently we are not getting enough information in Canada. We are told that the powers of Information Canada will be strengthened so as to provide a mechanism for disseminating the kind of information which is necessary. Well, some of the information which has been disseminated by that body certainly does not come within this ambit. If we can patriate the constitution, well and good; but not until changes can be brought about in the Victoria charter which will meet general agreement.
I shall conclude by dealing with certain recent activities in the field of foreign affairs. We did not get a chance to discuss foreign affairs while the present leader of the House was foreign minister. Foreign affairs during that period were as foreign as the constitution of Timbuktu.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: There was more debate during my time than at any other time.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There was none whatsoever, except in the most general way. The other day Mr. Ivan Head let the cat out of the bag and I think the time has come to say to him, "Ivan, ho. Stop. Whoa." He has no business whatsoever to be enunciating policy. I do not normally mention civil servants, but I cannot forget that Mr. Ivan Head wrote the introduction to a book of speeches by the Prime Minister and pronounced them to be pure poetry. And he had written them himself! What is the situation? The Prime Minister cannot be permitted to get away with the idea that he can deny that Ivan Head expressed himself regarding the new leftward turn in foreign affairs in Canada. I will read a few excerpts. These are from the Canadian Press:
Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau is determined to give Canada a strong, new activist role on the left wing of international affairs, Ivan Head, Mr. Trudeau's special foreign affairs adviser, said Wednesday.
With the help of Allan MacEachen as his new external affairs minister, Mr. Trudeau will seek to heighten Canada's world influence by taking a more moralistic approach to world problems.
Do you have to be on the left to be moralistic?
The new emphasis will be on the human problems affecting people wherever they live and on strengthening Canada's ties with Europe, Japan and the developing countries of Asia and Africa.
That is Mr. Head speaking, and Mr. Head knows. He went on to say the Prime Minister will be making many visits abroad. He will be visiting the Swedish Prime Minister who, Mr. Head said, has greatly impressed the right hon. gentleman with his "outspoken left-wing approach to international problems. According to this report, Mr. Head went on to say that the Swedes, with their denunciation of the Viet Nam war and the military revolt in Chile, had

October 3, 1974
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker become "the cutting edge of the left-very active, outspoken and moral." The report adds:
Canada can be expected to take a similar, though not necessarily identical, approach to such problems in the future, he said.
And a little later:
Mr. Head said Mr. Trudeau met the Swedish prime minister in Austria last winter and was keenly interested in learning more about Sweden's activist foreign policy.
Mr. Head did say there was a leftist turn. Indeed, the day before he spoke to the Canadian Press reporter there was a dispatch from the United Nations under the heading "MacEachen to initiate shift in foreign policy". This is an article by Duart Farquharson in which we find the following:
External affairs minister Allan MacEachen believes a renewed era of tough U.S. bargaining with Canada may have already begun-
In the same article, the following is stated:
Canada's image abroad, so far as it is reflected in the personal characteristics of its new spokesman to the world, is also in for a change.
They infer that from his transfer from House leader to minister of foreign affairs, because apparently he cannot be pushed around by "Heads". The article continues:
Turning to Canada's relations with the rest of the world, the external affairs minister confirmed in broad terms a recent report out of the prime minister's office that the Trudeau-MacEachen foreign policy will be to seek a strong, new active role on the left wing of international affairs.
That is a report from New York of what the minister said. But the Prime Minister says that Mr. Head never said the same thing. When Mr. Head gets a full head of steam, one never knows what he will say when it comes to leftist ideas. I am not satisfied with the position in which this very reliable young reporter has been placed. He is in the position of having it look like he had written something that was fiction. What is the foreign policy of this country with reference to leftist turns? Why should we not know that? Is this a radical departure from current policy which has never received the support of public opinion, which has never been discussed nationally and which has never been dealt with in this place, where foreign policy views should be accepted?
Because there is so much approval of the committee system, I make the suggestion that the foreign affairs committee be called together-and I should like to be a member of it, if I might be chosen for this purpose-so that Mr. Head can be given the opportunity to state what he has said, rather than hearing these alibis for his statements. What did he say, and where are we going? Is Canada taking a turn to the left? Does all this result from what the Prime Minister of Canada said when in Russia speaking to Sacha Kosygin, that we in Canada fear the United States economically-and we do-that we fear the United States culturally-and we do-and that we even fear the United States militarily? Is it any wonder that our relations with the United States today are at their lowest ebb?
It has now been revealed that the CIA has been upsetting governments, undermining governments and giving bonuses to those it has been helping. This is something I

have said on other occasions since 1963 when the Liberal party was the beneficiary of the antagonism of the government of President Kennedy, when the president's chief lieutenant in relation to polls and the like, Mr. Harris, came to Toronto with a certain group, following which the Liberal Party found itself with endless funds during the last two weeks of the campaign. I could not understand that. There was also the interference which took place when General Norstad was sent here to say what Canada should do.
In addition, there were schools for pressmen, held by the United States Embassy, to give them the basis upon which to attack the government which I had the honour to lead. Why? Because we took the position that as the danger of air attack on America from the north no longer existed, there was no reason that we should extend the nuclear family. The United States itself had determined that in fact there was an end to the danger of attack from the north. We were reviled for that. The Liberal party turned a complete somersault following the visit of a former prime minister to New York. After his return in the month of January, he said in Scarborough that Canada should accept nuclear weapons. I would like this whole matter looked into.
We noticed the other day that the CIA revelations are not to cover the period 1959 to 1964. I should like to have some of these CIA individuals on the witness-stand before our foreign relations committee, so that they might have the opportunity of explaining whether Canada was one of the nations that received treatment similar to other nations in North America as a result of the unjustifiable and unnatural actions of the CIA. For this and other reasons I should like an opportunity to be provided for a discussion of foreign affairs in this House. Until we have had that opportunity of discussion, let Mr. Head keep his mouth shut, and those connected with external affairs not push Canada into a leftist position.
Where are we going? The minister was in New York the other day and he suggested that Mr. Moroz, a patriot who has committed no offence, like hundreds of thousands of others in the U.S.S.R. who have been put into mental hospitals and the like, is getting along fine and is enjoying good health. What manner of nonsense is it, that Canada does not speak out in the United Nations calling upon the U.S.S.R. to uphold the principles of the United Nations charter which provide for the right of self-determination and which deny those things contrary to every concept of democratic government? Why has Canada not spoken out? Why the silence, as well, regarding the three Baltic countries and the Ukraine? Why does Canada not speak out, instead of taking this attitude of saying nice things to the U.S.S.R.? Why does Canada not get down to asking that immortal question: How is Moroz getting along, and is his health good?

speechtext: That is an uncalled-for statement.

speechtext: Shame, e (i5io)
